title: THE TEN WOMEN DAVID NEVER TOUCHED AGAIN
paragraphs:
THE TEN WOMEN DAVID NEVER TOUCHED AGAIN
They were left behind to guard a palace. Then a prince used their bodies to seize a kingdom. When David finally came home, they would spend the rest of their lives behind closed doors. But if you think this story is only about ten forgotten women, keep reading—because buried inside their silence is a warning about sin, a picture of its devastating consequences, and ultimately a desperate human need that only Jesus Christ can answer.
There is a sentence in the Bible that is frightening precisely because Scripture does not slow down to make it frightening.
No thunder.
No long explanation.
No names.
Just ten women... and the rest of their lives compressed into a few devastating Hebrew words.
David had finally returned to Jerusalem after the rebellion of his son Absalom. The throne had survived. The palace was his again. The rebellion was collapsing into history.
You might expect celebration.
Instead, David walked back into his house and found ten living reminders of everything that had happened while he was gone.

Second Samuel 20:3 records that David took the ten concubines he had left behind, placed them in a guarded house, continued providing for them, never again had sexual relations with them, and that they remained confined until death, “living in widowhood.”
Read that again slowly.
Until.
Their.
Death.
The Hebrew is painfully stark:
צְרֻרוֹת עַד־יוֹם מֻתָן אַלְמְנוּת חַיּוּת
ṣərurōṯ ʿaḏ-yōm muṯān, ʾalmənūṯ ḥayyūṯ.

The key word צְרֻרוֹת — ṣərurōṯ carries the sense of being bound, restricted, shut up, or confined. Then comes אַלְמְנוּת — ʾalmənūṯ: widowhood. The Hebrew text portrays women who remained restricted until the day of their death, living in a state of widowhood.
But here is where we must be careful.
The Bible tells us what David did.
It does not explicitly give us a sentence saying, “David did this because…”
That distinction matters.
We should never make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
But the events leading to that locked house reveal why their situation had become so tragic.
And to understand those ten women behind those doors, you have to go backward.
Back to the day David ran.
Absalom, David's own son, had stolen the hearts of many Israelites and launched a rebellion against his father. Jerusalem became unsafe. David fled the capital with his household.
But not everyone went with him.
Second Samuel 15:16 tells us:
עֶשֶׂר נָשִׁים פִּלַגְשִׁים לִשְׁמֹר הַבָּיִת
ʿeśer nāšîm pilagšîm lišmōr habbāyiṯ.
“Ten women, concubines, to keep the house.”
The Hebrew לִשְׁמֹר — lišmōr, from shamar, means to keep, watch, guard, preserve, or attend to.
David left these ten women behind to care for the palace.
Think about that.
They were not introduced as conspirators.
Scripture never tells us they joined Absalom's rebellion.
It never tells us they betrayed David.
They were left behind.
Ten women in a palace belonging to a king who had fled from his own son.
Then Absalom entered Jerusalem.
And one of the darkest political strategies in David's story was proposed.

Ahithophel advised Absalom to have relations with his father's concubines. The purpose stated in the text was brutally political: Israel would hear of it, the rupture between father and son would become unmistakable, and Absalom's supporters would become more resolute. Then a tent was erected on the palace roof, and Absalom went in to his father's concubines “in the sight of all Israel.”
The Hebrew makes the public humiliation unmistakable:
לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל
ləʿênê kol-Yiśrāʾēl.
“Before the eyes of all Israel.”
They had been left to watch a house.
Now their bodies had become part of a public declaration of rebellion.
That distinction matters.

The narrative explicitly describes Ahithophel's political purpose and Absalom's action. It does not record the women's consent, motives, words, or perspective. We therefore should not invent details the text does not give us.
We should not pretend to know what they said.
We should not manufacture dialogue.
We should not accuse them of willingly participating when Scripture does not tell us that.
What Scripture gives us is already horrifying enough.
A powerful man used access to women associated with the king as a public weapon against his father.
And there was another layer to this tragedy.
Years earlier, David himself had stood on a rooftop.
From there he saw Bathsheba.
What followed was adultery, pregnancy, deception, the arranged death of Uriah, and one of the greatest moral collapses in David's life.
When Nathan confronted him, David finally said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
David was forgiven.
But forgiveness did not mean his actions produced no earthly consequences.

Nathan had warned David that calamity would rise from within his own household and that what David had done secretly would be answered by public humiliation involving his household. Second Samuel itself later connects Absalom's rooftop act with that terrible trajectory.
And suddenly the rooftop becomes haunting.
David's hidden sexual sin began its terrible chain of consequences around a rooftop.
Years later, his family's sexual disgrace became public on a rooftop.
Sin has echoes.
That does not mean the ten women deserved what happened to them.
They did not become morally guilty simply because David had sinned.
And this is precisely where careless preaching can become cruel.
The consequences of one person's sin can crash into the lives of people who did not create that sin.
A father's choices can wound children.
A husband's secret can devastate a wife.
A leader's corruption can injure an entire congregation.
A parent's addiction can shape a child's childhood.
One person's lust can leave another person carrying memories for decades.
Sin is personal.
But sin is rarely private.
Maybe that is why this ancient story feels disturbingly modern.
Because perhaps you know what it is like to live inside consequences you did not start.
Maybe somebody else's decision changed your life.
Maybe somebody walked away and you had to live with what remained.
Maybe someone used you.
Maybe somebody with more power than you made a decision, and you became collateral damage.
Maybe your name was never mentioned.
Maybe everyone remembers the scandal but nobody remembers what happened to you afterward.
That is one of the most painful things about these ten women.
We know David.
We know Absalom.
We know Ahithophel.
But Scripture does not give us the names of these ten women.
Ten lives.
Ten stories.
Ten human beings.
Unnamed.
And after the rebellion ended, David came home.
Imagine the palace gates opening.
Imagine servants returning.
Imagine rooms being restored.
The king is back.
The kingdom survived.
The crisis is over.
Except for them.
For them, the story did not simply go back to normal.
David placed them in a guarded residence. He provided for their material needs. He no longer had relations with them. They remained there until death, living as widows.
Why?
Again, Scripture does not explicitly state David's reasoning, so humility is necessary.

We can observe important biblical background. Sexual relations with one's father's wife were expressly forbidden in Israel's law; Deuteronomy 22:30 prohibits taking one's father's wife and uses the Hebrew idiom of uncovering the father's garment. Absalom's action was therefore not merely provocative politics. It was a profound violation of the family order established in the law.

David's response afterward appears to recognize that something irreversible had happened to the women's place within his household. He continued to support them, but he did not resume sexual relations with them.
Yet we must resist turning that observation into a divine endorsement of everything David did.
This is crucial.
The Bible frequently records human actions without commanding them.
David was a man after God's own heart in the biblical story, but David was not the standard of sinless righteousness.
Jesus is.
David could write psalms and still fail.
David could worship deeply and still make catastrophic decisions.
David could repent sincerely and still leave wounded people in the wake of his sin.
And that is one reason the Bible is so believable.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
Scripture does not hand David to us with perfect lighting.
It gives us the shepherd.
The giant killer.
The fugitive.
The king.
The worshiper.
The adulterer.
The schemer.
The grieving father.
The repentant sinner.
The forgiven man who still had to watch consequences walk through his house.
Because the Bible was never ultimately trying to convince you that David could save you.
David needed saving too.
And so do we.
This is where those locked doors in Jerusalem eventually point us beyond David.
Because another Son of David was coming.
Jesus Christ.
David possessed a kingdom and could not keep his own household from collapsing.
Jesus receives a kingdom that will never end.
David's sin brought pain into the lives of others.
Jesus committed no sin, yet willingly carried the sins of others.
David returned to Jerusalem after his son died and found a household scarred by rebellion.
Jesus went outside Jerusalem and died for rebels.
Do you see the reversal?
We rebelled.
He was wounded.
We sinned.
He bore judgment.
We wandered.
He came looking for the lost.
We accumulated shame.
He carried shame to a cross.
And when Jesus rose from the grave, He did not merely offer sinners better behavior.
He offered new life.
This is the Gospel.
Not that your past never happened.
Not that consequences magically disappear.
Not that wounds are imaginary.
Not that every broken earthly relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
The Gospel is greater than pretending.
The Gospel declares that sin does not get the final word over everyone who belongs to Jesus Christ.
There are things Christ forgives that you still remember.
There are scars grace does not require you to deny.
There are consequences you may still have to walk through after genuine repentance.
But there is a difference between living with consequences and living under condemnation.
For the person who is in Christ, condemnation does not own the ending.
That is why David's story must never become an excuse for David's sin.
It must become a warning about ours.
Maybe you have spent years saying, “Nobody knows.”
David once had a secret too.
Maybe the hidden relationship has not been discovered.
Maybe the messages are still deleted.
Maybe the pornography is still hidden behind a password.
Maybe bitterness has become so normal that you no longer call it hatred.
Maybe pride has learned Christian vocabulary.
Maybe everybody at church thinks you are strong.
Maybe your family thinks you are fine.
Maybe your followers see Scripture on your profile while God sees something completely different when the screen goes dark.
Do not wait for your rooftop.
Bring the secret into the light before sin drags it there.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God's mercy calling you home before rebellion finishes what it started.
David's confession after Nathan confronted him was not complicated:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
Sometimes restoration begins when excuses finally die.
Not, “I sinned because my marriage was difficult.”
Not, “I sinned because I was lonely.”
Not, “I sinned because everybody does it.”
Not, “I sinned because they tempted me.”
Just...
I sinned.
And I need mercy.
That is the doorway grace walks through.
Perhaps, though, you are reading this from the other side.
You were not David.
You were one of the people caught in somebody else's fallout.
Then hear this carefully.
What somebody did to you is not the same thing as who you are.
Human beings may reduce people to scandals.
Jesus does not.
People may remember the worst chapter.
Christ sees the person standing inside it.
People may know you by what happened to you.
Jesus knows you by name.
And no locked room on earth can prevent Christ from seeing the person inside.

The ten concubines disappear from the biblical narrative after this verse. Scripture gives us no later account of their individual lives, thoughts, deaths, or spiritual condition. We should honor that silence rather than invent sentimental endings for them.
But their silence still teaches us something.
There are people living quietly with the aftermath of somebody else's choices.
People sitting beside you in church.
People smiling in family photographs.
People answering “I'm okay.”
People who survived something they still cannot comfortably explain.
People whose greatest battles will never become testimonies on a stage.
And followers of Jesus should be the kind of people who notice them.
Not exploit their stories.
Not gossip about their wounds.
Not make entertainment from their humiliation.
Notice them.
Protect dignity.
Tell truth.
Seek justice.
Practice mercy.
Carry burdens.
Point wounded people toward Christ.
Because Jesus never built His kingdom by using vulnerable people as political objects.
He welcomed the overlooked.
He touched the untouchable.
He ate with the despised.
He confronted hypocrites.
He called sinners to repentance.
He received the broken.
And then He stretched His own hands across a Roman cross.
This is why Christianity cannot finally be reduced to “be more like David.”
No.
We need Someone greater than David.
We need the true King.
We need Jesus.
The One who does not merely expose darkness but rescues sinners from it.
The One who does not call evil good, yet still welcomes the guilty who repent.
The One whose blood is sufficient for adulterers, liars, hypocrites, rebels, the ashamed, the wounded, and people who thought they had gone too far.
Maybe you came to this article wondering why ten ancient concubines spent their remaining years in seclusion.
But perhaps the question following you now is different.
What is the hidden thing in my life doing to the people around me?
Or perhaps:
How long will I allow what somebody did to me to convince me that my story is over?
Either question can bring you to Jesus.
Be sincere before God. Turn to Christ.
Someone reading the comments may realize for the first time that they are not the only person fighting to believe again.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Send it privately to the person who feels permanently stained by their past.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, or keep your eyes on Jesus, follow and stay close.

Supporting Gospel ministry should never be presented as purchasing God's favor. We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, love, generosity, truth, worship, and good works—not through a commercial transaction.
Your support can help Gospel-centered teaching travel farther, and your share may put the message in front of the one person in your circle who would never have searched for it themselves.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Forgiveness does not come with a price tag you can afford.
Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So share because truth matters.
Support Gospel work because you freely want others to hear.
Give because you love Christ, not because someone frightened you into believing God will love you more.
Follow because your soul needs Scripture more than your feed needs another distraction.
The ten women of Second Samuel 20:3 eventually vanished from the pages of recorded history.
But their verse remains.
A locked house.
A king carrying consequences.
Ten unnamed women living in widowhood.
A family devastated by rebellion.
A throne that could not heal the damage underneath it.
And centuries later...
another King entered Jerusalem.
He wore no crown of gold that day.
They gave Him thorns.
He did not climb onto a rooftop to display somebody else's shame.
He climbed Golgotha carrying ours.
He did not use wounded people to secure His throne.
He gave Himself for wounded people and sinners while possessing a throne no rebellion could ultimately take away.
That is our hope.
Your scandal may explain a chapter.
Your wounds may shape a chapter.
Your failures may haunt a chapter.
Other people's sins may have torn pages you desperately wish you could rewrite.
But none of them deserves to be worshiped as the author of your ending.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Jesus still receives the repentant.
Jesus still restores what sin tried to own.
Jesus still brings people out of darkness.
Jesus still writes grace where human beings expected only shame.
And maybe the most haunting thing about those ten locked-away women is not merely that history forgot their names.
Maybe it is the reminder that Jesus never overlooks the person everyone else remembers only as part of the scandal.
Your darkest chapter does not get to hold the pen when your life has been surrendered to Christ.
